tasks.task_description: Requirement 1: A brief assessment (<=2 pages in the original framing) of the three options available to the Zambezi River Authority for addressing the deteriorating Kariba Dam — (1) repair the existing dam, (2) rebuild the existing dam, (3) remove Kariba and replace it with a series of 10-20 smaller dams along the upper Zambezi. The goal is to give ZRA management an overview of the potential costs and benefits of each option so a direction can be chosen, and to motivate the detailed analysis of Option 3 in Requirement 2.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (a) the 2015 Institute of Risk Management of South Africa finding that Kariba is 'in dire need of maintenance' holds, so the status quo (no action) is not a viable option; (b) all three options must deliver the same core services — hydropower, flood control, water supply, and navigation/irrigation support — for a like-for-like cost-benefit comparison; (c) costs are compared at a planning-estimate level (order-of-magnitude, ~2017 USD) because detailed engineering cost data are not available, so relative ranking matters more than absolute figures; (d) benefits are assessed over a common 50-year analysis horizon with a 7% discount rate. Method: a structured cost-benefit screening. For each option I enumerate capital cost, annual O&M, residual risk, service continuity during the works, and socio-environmental impact, then score them against the requirement to keep Kariba's water-management capability in place. The three options are not equivalent in risk: repair leaves the existing failure mode (concrete arch, single point of failure) in place; rebuild removes it but at the cost of a full impoundment outage and a single large construction risk; Option 3 replaces one high-consequence asset with a distributed system of smaller, lower-consequence assets (the cascade logic developed in Requirement 2). This risk-reduction argument is the key differentiator and is carried into the detailed analysis.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Cost model (planning estimates, 2017 USD): let C_rep, C_reb, C_cas be the capital costs. Repair: C_rep ~ 0.15-0.25 x original construction cost (structural remediation, seepage control, spillway and turbine upgrades) — order $1-2B, because it reuses the existing 128 m arch and 180 km3 lake. Rebuild: C_reb ~ 0.8-1.2 x a new dam of comparable capacity — order $8-15B, plus a multi-year impoundment outage. Option 3 (from Requirement 2): C_cas ~ $166B is NOT the right comparison basis at this level; for the screening I use the relative form C_cas = N*($0.3B fixed + $0.9B/km3) with N in 10-20 and total working storage ~180 km3, giving a planning range of ~$160-250B if built to full Kariba storage, but a reduced-scope cascade (total working storage 100-130 km3) costs ~$110-140B. Annual O&M: O&M_rep ~ 1.5-2% of C_rep (high, due to ongoing monitoring of an aging structure); O&M_reb ~ 0.8-1% of C_reb (new structure); O&M_cas ~ 0.8-1% per dam but with N=14 sites, total O&M is comparable to a single large dam while per-site consequence is far lower. Risk term: expected loss = probability of failure x consequence. A single 128 m arch has a small but non-zero failure probability with an extreme consequence (downstream inundation of the whole valley, loss of the 180 km3 lake); a cascade of 14 dams each ~45 m high has a much lower per-dam consequence, and the probability that the SYSTEM loses flood control is the probability of a correlated multi-dam failure, which is far smaller. Benefit continuity: repair and rebuild both require the lake to be drawn down or the dam taken out of service for years, interrupting hydropower and water supply; Option 3 can be built incrementally (dams commissioned in sequence) so the river's water-management capability is maintained throughout. Scoring: a weighted score S = w1*(benefit continuity) + w2*(risk reduction) + w3*(cost), with weights reflecting ZRA's stated priority on safety. Resulting ranking: Option 3 (best on risk reduction and continuity, worst on absolute cost), Option 2 (best long-run structural integrity, large cost and outage), Option 1 (cheapest but leaves the failure mode and does not address the root maintenance deficit).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Findings: (1) Repair is the cheapest near-term fix (~$1-2B) but is a delay, not a solution — it does not remove the single-point-of-failure risk that triggered the 2015 warning, and O&M remains high because the aging structure must be continuously monitored. It buys time but defers the capital decision. (2) Rebuild (~$8-15B) produces a new, reliable single dam but at 5-10x the repair cost, with a multi-year impoundment outage that interrupts all services, and it concentrates the same high consequence in one asset. (3) Option 3 has the highest absolute cost in the full-storage case (~$160-250B) but uniquely delivers (a) a step-change in risk reduction by replacing one high-consequence dam with 14 low-consequence dams, (b) continuous service during a sequenced build, and (c) greater operational flexibility (per-dam release control). At a reduced storage scope (100-130 km3, still within the 10-20 dam envelope) the cost falls to ~$110-140B while retaining most of the risk and flexibility benefits. Recommendation from this screening: pursue Option 3 as the primary direction (it is the only option that structurally reduces the risk that motivated the review), with Option 2 as the fallback if the distributed capital cost is not fundable, and Option 1 only as a short-term interim measure to keep Kariba safe while the Option 3 decision is made. Limitations: the cost figures are planning estimates with wide bands (the true driver is the total storage decision, which Requirement 2 resolves); the risk comparison uses qualitative consequence ranking rather than a quantified fragility model; and the 50-year horizon and 7% discount rate are assumptions that could shift the ranking if ZRA uses a different social discount rate. The screening's purpose is directional — to justify concentrating the detailed analysis on Option 3 — not to produce a bankable estimate.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 2: A detailed analysis of Option 3 — removing Kariba and replacing it with a series of 10-20 smaller dams along the upper Zambezi that collectively provide the same overall water-management capabilities as the existing Kariba Dam (and the same or greater protection for the Lake Kariba area). The analysis must (a) recommend the number and placement of the new dams, (b) provide a flow-modulation strategy balancing safety and cost that handles the normal water cycle and emergency conditions (flooding and prolonged low water), with specific guidance from maximum to minimum expected discharge, and (c) state restrictions on the locations and durations for which different river reaches may be exposed to the most detrimental effects of the extreme conditions.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions and data (from the provided empirical dataset, cited in data/external_data.md): Lake Kariba total storage ~180 km3, length ~280 km, surface area ~5,400-5,580 km2, max depth ~97 m; mean annual inflow to Kariba ~51.5 km3/yr; mean annual discharge at Kariba 1,313.6 m3/s; pre-dam seasonal cycle with a Feb-Mar peak of ~5,000-20,000 m3/s (up to ~10,000 m3/s recorded at Victoria Falls in 1958) and an Oct-Nov low of ~200-800 m3/s (natural low ~230 m3/s at the Kariba section); upstream catchment ~679,000 km2. Modeling decisions, settled with the expert over three rounds: (R1) the problem is formulated as a SYSTEM-LEVEL CASCADE — the N dams are one coordinated series-storage system, not N independent projects — because the count/placement recommendation and the flood-attenuation behavior are system properties; (R2) 'same overall water management capabilities' is interpreted as FUNCTIONAL EQUIVALENCE (matching delivered services at the Lake-Kariba reference section) rather than matching a storage volume, with working-storage and gross-storage equivalence retained as sensitivity bounds; (R3) the equivalence benchmark is Kariba's own DELIVERED performance (calibrated by simulating the existing dam), with the 2015-warning flood-safety margin imposed as a binding constraint. A key structural finding emerged: a series cascade cannot replicate a single reservoir's dry-season flow-RAISING at equal total storage, because a single reservoir concentrates all storage at the release point while a cascade distributes it upstream of the reference section. This is reported as a genuine property/limitation of Option 3. Method: a monthly water-balance simulation of the cascade over a 30-year (360-month) seasonal hydrograph, with linear reservoir routing at each dam and a seasonal operating rule (flood / normal / drought). The total working storage is anchored to Lake Kariba's ~180 km3 (the empirical dataset explicitly identifies this as the benchmark for 'same overall water management capabilities'), distributed over N identical dams with a per-dam height limit (working storage <= 13 km3, a ~45 m gravity-arch proxy), which forces N >= 14. Among feasible N the system is chosen to minimize capital cost.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Hydrograph: monthly mean flows (m3/s) shaped to the documented cycle and normalized to the 1,313.6 m3/s annual mean: Jan 3200, Feb 5200, Mar 4600, Apr 2200, May 1000, Jun 520, Jul 380, Aug 330, Sep 280, Oct 230, Nov 400, Dec 1100 (rescaled so the 12-month mean equals 1,313.6). Tiled over 30 years (360 monthly steps, 30-day timesteps). Cascade state: S_j(t) = working storage of dam j (j=1..N upstream to downstream). Per dam per month, linear reservoir routing: S_t = S_j + I_j (inflow to dam j); release R = min(T, S_t) where T is the seasonal target release; spill SP = max(0, S_t - R - 0.92*C) (spillway activates above 92% of working storage C); S_j = S_t - R - SP; outflow to the next dam = R + SP. Seasonal target T per dam: flood months (inflow > 2*Q_MEAN = 2627 m3/s): T = Q_MEAN/N (release base load only, hold the surplus -> attenuation); drought months (inflow < 0.5*Q_MEAN = 657 m3/s): T = 350/N (draw storage to lift the system release toward the 350 m3/s dry-season target); normal months: T = Q_MEAN/N (base load, bank the surplus). Decision variables: N in {10..20}, per-dam working storage C = 180/N km3, constraint C <= 13 km3 (so N >= 14 is feasible). Objective: minimize capital cost Cost(N) = N*$0.3B + (180 km3)*$0.9B/km3. Service targets (from R3, Kariba's calibrated delivered values): peak outlet release <= Kariba's 4216 m3/s (the <=3000 m3/s 2015-warning margin is reported as a stretch goal requiring extra spillway capacity); mean annual outlet release >= ~1200 m3/s (no net water loss vs the 1313.6 natural mean); dry-season (Jul-Sep) mean outlet release >= 350 m3/s. Calibrated Kariba baseline (single 180 km3 dam, same hydrograph, standard operating rules): peak 4216 m3/s, mean 1234 m3/s, dry-season mean 400 m3/s. Natural (no-dam) Kariba-section values: peak ~5200 m3/s, mean 1313.6 m3/s, dry-season mean ~350 m3/s. Results of the optimization (total working storage fixed at 180 km3): N=14 is the minimum-cost feasible system — 14 dams, 12.9 km3 working storage each, spaced 20.0 km apart along the 280 km upper-river segment, capital cost ~$166B. It delivers peak 4216 m3/s (matches Kariba, 19% below the natural 5200), mean 1233 m3/s (matches Kariba), and dry-season mean 350 m3/s (at the natural level, below Kariba's raised 400 — the structural cascade limitation). N=15..20 are feasible and slightly more expensive ($166.5-168.0B) with marginally better 3-month low-flow minima; N=10..13 are infeasible because 180/N km3 per dam exceeds the 13 km3 height limit. Flow-modulation strategy (operating rule): base load per dam = 1313.6/14 = 93.8 m3/s in normal operation; in flood the dams hold surplus and pass only base load (attenuating the seasonal peak), keeping storage at or below 92% with 30% minimum freeboard from December through April; in drought the dams draw down to lift the system release to 350 m3/s, never below a 25% working-storage resilience floor. Extreme-flow guidance: maximum expected inflow ~5200 m3/s (seasonal peak) is attenuated to a 4216 m3/s outlet peak; the 10,000 m3/s Victoria Falls design flood (which affects the lower river) is handled by the upper-dam freeboard and spillways with the lower cascade passing a controlled fraction; minimum expected inflow ~230 m3/s (natural dry low) is supplemented by storage release to the 350 m3/s dry-season target for the 3-month Jul-Sep window. Exposure restrictions: flood exposure is concentrated in the upper reaches (dams 1-5, km 0-100), which see the unattenuated seasonal peak, and is spread and attenuated downstream by ~1-2 weeks per 3-4 dams; the peak-exposure window is ~6-8 weeks (Feb-Mar). Drought/drawdown exposure is greatest in the lower reaches (dams 10-14, km 180-280), because upstream storage has already been released; the critical 3-month low-flow window is Aug-Sep. Restrictions: no reach may be drawn below 25% of working storage for more than one consecutive dry season, and flood freeboard (the top 8% of storage) must be kept clear from December through April.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommendation: build 14 dams, each with ~12.9 km3 of working storage (~45 m equivalent height), evenly spaced at ~20 km along the 280 km upper-river segment (km 0, 20, 40, ..., 260, with the 14th near the former Kariba site), for a total working storage of 180 km3 matched to Lake Kariba and a planning capital cost of ~$166B. This system matches Kariba's delivered flood protection (4216 m3/s peak vs 4216) and mean-flow regulation (1233 vs 1234 m3/s), reduces the downstream peak by ~19% relative to the natural 5200 m3/s seasonal peak, and sustains a 350 m3/s dry-season mean. The laddered placement provides the distributed-risk benefit: no single dam failure loses the system's flood control, and the sequenced build maintains service throughout construction. Sensitivity (R2 bounds): at the working-storage bound (60% of Kariba = 108 km3) the system would need N>=9 and smaller dams but would lose ~40% of the drought-resilience storage; at the gross-storage bound (180 km3, the chosen anchor) it is fully functional; the 100%-gross case confirms 180 km3 is the storage needed for functional equivalence. Limitations and bias analysis: (1) The cascade sustains a 350 m3/s dry-season mean rather than Kariba's raised 400 — a real, structural service gap from distributing storage upstream of the reference section; closing it would require disproportionate additional storage and is not cost-justified, so ZRA should treat the 50 m3/s dry-season gap as the price of the distributed-risk design. (2) The <=3000 m3/s flood margin from the 2015 warning is not met (the system delivers 4216, Kariba-parity); achieving 3000 would require larger spillways on the upper dams or a larger first dam, at added cost — flagged as a stretch goal. (3) The model uses a deterministic seasonal hydrograph (no interannual stochasticity in the final sizing run) and a linear routing rule, so the 30-year mean behavior is well captured but single-event flood routing (the shape and timing of an individual 10,000 m3/s pulse) is only approximately represented; a daily-resolution event simulation would refine the peak-attenuation figure. (4) Per-dam cost is a planning proxy ($0.3B fixed + $0.9B/km3); actual costs vary with geology, access, and resettlement, which the even-spacing placement assumes away. (5) The 280 km placement length and 13 km3 height limit are proxies for the actual valley geometry; detailed siting would shift individual dam locations but not the N=14, 180 km3 conclusion. Overall, the analysis supports Option 3 as viable and risk-reducing, with the recommended 14-dam / 180 km3 / 20-km-spacing system as the baseline design and the flow-modulation rule (base load 93.8 m3/s/dam, flood-hold with 30% freeboard, drought-draw to 350 m3/s with a 25% floor) as the operating strategy, subject to the two flagged service gaps (dry-season raising and the 3000 m3/s flood margin) that ZRA should weigh against the distributed-risk and construction-continuity benefits.
